narratives.title: The Weekly Report Nobody Trusts
narratives.angle: Lead with the specific frustration of preparing weekly performance reports where inventory figures are doubted, and the hours lost to manual checks between systems.
narratives.coreMessage: When your weekly report needs a hand-check before anyone acts on it, the data quality problem is sitting in your operations, not your IT department.
supportingThemes: The hidden hours spent reconciling inventory against order records by hand
Why mismatches between systems end up on the operations leader's desk
What happens to decisions when weekly figures have to be verified first
What a trustworthy warehouse report looks like without a dedicated data team
narratives.audienceFit: These leaders are personally accountable for weekly reporting and lack data teams, so they feel the daily cost of untrusted numbers and manual reconciliation.
evidenceRequirements: ref-survey to support claims about trust in weekly inventory figures
ref-benchmark to support claims about time spent on manual reconciliation
ref-product to describe how scheduled checks flag mismatches for human review
risks: Could drift into fear-mongering about data chaos, violating the no fear-mongering rule
Might imply the product fixes records automatically when it only flags them [ref-product]
Must avoid prohibited words like 'guarantee' when describing report reliability

narratives.title: Data Quality is an Operations Problem
narratives.angle: Argue that data quality shows up in the weekly report and delays real warehouse decisions, not in server logs, repositioning it as an operations issue.
narratives.coreMessage: Data quality is an operations problem because it appears in your weekly report and slows down real decisions, not just in the server room.
supportingThemes: Why the weekly performance report is where data quality becomes visible
The difference between system uptime and trustworthy operational numbers
How flagging mismatches for a person to review keeps warehouse records under human control
Starting a conversation about which numbers you actually trust in your current reporting
narratives.audienceFit: Operations leaders without IT teams need to own this issue directly; framing it as operations rather than IT matches their accountability for weekly results.
evidenceRequirements: ref-survey to evidence that 62% of operations leaders distrust their weekly figures
ref-product to explain the scheduled check and human review process
Must include the terms 'data quality' and 'operations' per constraints
risks: Could sound preachy or abstract if not tied to concrete warehouse reporting situations
Risk of using marketing jargon instead of plain-spoken operations language
Must not imply the product changes records—it only flags mismatches [ref-product]

narratives.title: What 14 Warehouses and 120 Leaders Showed
narratives.angle: Lead with the specific survey and pilot figures to demonstrate this is a measurable problem with a practical solution, then connect to the product approach.
narratives.coreMessage: In a survey of 120 operations leaders, 62% said they did not fully trust the inventory figures in their weekly report [ref-survey], and in a pilot across 14 warehouses, teams using automated checks cut time spent on manual reconciliation by 31% [ref-benchmark]—showing data quality is a measurable operations issue.
supportingThemes: What the 62% figure means for how weekly reports get used in operations
How the 14-warehouse pilot actually ran: scheduled checks comparing records
Comparing hours spent on manual reconciliation before and after automated flags
Why mismatches get flagged for a person to review rather than changed automatically
narratives.audienceFit: Gives busy operations leaders concrete, specific numbers they can compare against their own reporting and reconciliation time.
evidenceRequirements: ref-survey for the 62% statistic about trust in inventory figures
ref-benchmark for the 31% reduction in manual reconciliation time across 14 warehouses
ref-product for the description of scheduled checks and human review
risks: Figures could be misread as universal guarantees rather than specific pilot and survey results
Must frame statistics as 'in a survey' and 'in a pilot' to avoid implying guaranteed outcomes
Cannot introduce any other numbers or comparisons not covered by the references
